content: In four randomized controlled trials, the mortality rate was 30 per 1,000, with a difference of 19 per 1,000, equating to 11 fewer deaths per 1,000 (95% confidence interval: 16 fewer to 4 fewer). The evidence quality was rated as high. The time to hospital discharge, based on data from 113 participants in three randomized controlled trials, showed moderate certainty due to serious imprecision. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for malaria, updated on October 16, 2023, reported that 427 out of 451 standard doses of artesunate and quinine (with a loading dose) were used. In the artesunate group, eight participants were included. There was no serious imprecision, and the 95% confidence interval of the pooled effect suggested a clinically significant benefit with artesunate. The number needed to treat to prevent one childhood death was 38. However, there was a serious risk of bias, as 24% (41/170) of patients with neurological sequelae at discharge were not available for assessment at day 28. The trial was conducted across 11 centers in Africa, using standard dosing of artesunate and quinine. The nature of the neurological sequelae was not described, but the absolute effect confidence interval was narrow, indicating no serious imprecision. Neurological sequelae at day 28 increased by 2%, but the risk of bias was not serious. Allocation concealment was adequate in all trials, and the risk of bias was low. Although the trials were unblinded, this was unlikely to affect the objective outcomes. There was no statistical heterogeneity between trials (I² = 0%), and the data were primarily derived from a multicenter trial conducted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania. In Asia, five trials compared artesunate and quinine, with no statistical heterogeneity (I² = 0%). The trials included participants from Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam, with age groups over 15–16 years. Two smaller trials did not administer a loading dose of quinine, but this did not result in statistical heterogeneity compared to the larger multicenter trial where the loading dose was given. The effect estimate for artesunate indicated clinically important harm, but the 95% confidence interval included the possibility of no clinically significant difference between the two interventions. The trials were generally well-conducted, with low risk of bias, and no evidence of large differences between treatment groups. Neurological sequelae in adults following severe malaria were rare, but the 95% confidence interval included the possibility of clinically significant harm with artesunate. The large multicenter study adequately concealed allocation, while the smaller trial did not. Neither trial was blinded. In children with severe malaria, trials conducted in East and West Africa and India compared intramuscular artemether with intravenous quinine. Most trials used the WHO-recommended dose of quinine. The meta-analysis had adequate power to detect statistically significant effects, but the results were inconsistent. The mean difference in parasite clearance time ranged from a 2-hour increase with artemether to a 15-hour decrease. Mass testing and treatment (MTaT) interventions were evaluated in seven studies, including four cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) conducted in Kenya, Indonesia, Zambia, and Burkina Faso, and three non-randomized studies (NRSs) in Senegal, Ghana, and India. The cRCTs conducted 2–3 rounds of MTaT over one year, except for the Kenya study, which conducted six rounds over two years. Studies in Kenya and Burkina Faso were in moderate-to-high transmission areas, while those in Indonesia and Zambia were in low-transmission areas. The overall risk of bias for community-level outcomes in these studies was low. Meta-analyses found little to no reduction in community-level incidence or prevalence of infection, although two studies reported a small reduction in clinical malaria incidence. The certainty of evidence from the NRSs was graded as very low. MTaT did not significantly reduce malaria prevalence at two months, based on data from 3,660 participants in one study. Similarly, MTaT did not reduce the incidence of malaria infection between 0–12 months, based on data from 857 participants. However, MTaT reduced the incidence of clinical malaria between 0–12 months, based on data from 332,454 participants in two studies. Adverse events related to MTaT were evaluated in one study involving 6,373 participants. The evidence was very uncertain due to serious indirectness and imprecision. In summary, artesunate demonstrated significant clinical benefits in some settings, particularly in reducing mortality in children with severe malaria. However, the evidence for its impact on neurological sequelae and other outcomes was inconsistent. MTaT interventions showed limited effectiveness in reducing malaria prevalence or incidence at the community level, with very uncertain evidence regarding adverse events. Further research is needed to clarify these findings and optimize malaria treatment and prevention strategies.
